Lightning Class — Niantic Bay

A 19 ft Lightning sloop racing on the real Niantic Bay, Connecticut — and the chart she races on is a photograph of the real bay from the air.

International Lightning Class Association — www.lightningclass.org

Simulation Tutorial · What is a Lightning ?

Voice commands (optional — switch the microphone on with the button below, or with M at any time during the race)
“come about”T — the bow goes through the wind
“jibe”J — the stern goes through the wind

Lightning Class — Niantic Bay

A two-player online race for 19 ft Lightning sloops: in the pre-start the host lays the whole course — the windward mark W, the leeward mark L and both ends of the starting line, the orange starting mark S and the committee boat — then both boats start behind that line, beat to the windward mark W and round it leaving it to port, run off to the leeward mark L and round that to port too, then finish by crossing the line again — either way through it. Once the gun has gone and both boats are across the line, the host may drag that line again: the same line is the finish line, and where he leaves it is where they finish. One minute sequence - a horn at 60 seconds, an air horn beep at 10 seconds and then at 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1, the cannon at the gun with a plume of smoke off the committee boat's gun, and the loud cannon and the cheering for the first boat home. The host sets the wind too; it shifts and gusts around the bay in patches a few hundred metres across. He also sets the pace: a time factor from 1 to 5 under the wind panel speeds the boats up - and only the boats. The clock, the wind and the water keep real time.

How boat speed is worked out

The Lightning is a 19 ft one-design: a narrow, flat-bottomed, hard-chined centreboarder with a big rig, and everything on this card is here because it decides how fast the two boats on the chart can go. Nothing on it is a guess about the real bay - the bay's own geography comes from the chart's sources - but some of the numbers the model needs are not published, and those are labelled as assumptions.

Published class data

International Lightning Class Association: LOA 19'0" (5.80 m) · LWL 15.25 ft (4.65 m) · beam 6'6" (2.00 m) · bare hull 700 lb (318 kg) · main + jib 177 ft² (16.4 m²) · spinnaker 300 ft² (27.9 m²) · mast 26'2" (7.9 m) · crew 3 · Portsmouth D-PN 87.0.

Class speed file: hull speed 5.23 kn = 1.34√LWL, and a planing band in length Froude number FnL 0.70 / 0.89 / 1.10 = 9.2 / 11.7 / 14.4 kn. 14 kn is the top of the credible band, so 14 kn is the model's cap.

Model polar at this wind

Planing, and not planing

Below FnL 0.70 (9.2 kn) she is a displacement boat: the faster she is pushed the more of a wave she has to climb, so the curve is steep and the upwind speeds of a beat sit near hull speed, around 5 kn. Between 0.70 and 1.10 the hull is coming out of its own wave - the hump - and drag rises fastest exactly where drive rises slowest, which is why the transition is where the two boats on the chart lose most of their gains. Above FnL 1.10 she is planing, her wetted length and area fall as she rises, and the same sail force buys much more speed - that is the whole reason a Lightning can sail a run at 14 kn under a spinnaker when her hull speed is 5.2.

What the model does with that

Hull drag, planing. Savitsky (1964) planing-hull resistance above FnL 0.6, on the class's chine beam of 1.80 m, 8° deadrise and 3° running trim.
Hull drag, not planing. Below that, ITTC-1957 friction on 7.0 m² of wetted surface with a 1.20 form factor, plus a residuary hump peaking at Fn 0.47 - the branch the planing relations do not cover. The two are blended across FnL 0.6-1.0, so nothing snaps at the join.
Heel. Extra drag from heel in proportion to the excess of heel beyond a knee: the crew's 3.3 kN of righting moment is what balances the rig, and a boat pinned over is slower - which is why the boat eases as she heels, as on the water.
The rig. Each sail is a low-aspect-ratio lifting surface: effective aspect ratio 4.5 for the main and the jib (the boom and the water end-plate them), 1.6 for the kite; a stalled sail loses its drive, and the kite both fills above about 55° apparent and hurts on a reach.
Drive = drag. For a given wind, heading and trim, the model sweeps both sheets and solves drive against hull drag for the speed where they balance. That is where the polar table above comes from: the speed at the best trim, kite down and kite set, for this wind.
The cap. Nothing in the game sails faster than the class file's 14 kn, whatever the polar would prefer in a gust.
Assumptions (labelled, not class measurements). Chine beam 1.80 m, deadrise 8°, running trim 3°, sailing weight 570 kg (318 kg hull + three crew), wetted surface 7.0 m², form factor 1.20, residuary peak 0.035 W at Fn 0.47, non-hull drag allowance 15% of the drag when not planing and 12% when planing, max righting moment 500 kg·m, sail plan centre of effort 4.2 m above the water.
Not modelled. Waves, current, chop, and the boat's own pitch and roll: the water on the chart moves and changes colour with the wind, but it does not slow her down.

Controls and rules
← / → turn 1° to port / starboard: one tap is one degree of helm, and holding the key keeps her coming at her own rate until you let go
T come about: the bow goes through the wind (the command is spoken “come about”, not “tack”)
J jibe: the stern goes through the wind
Either one leaves her symmetric on the opposite tack - same angle off the wind, other side - and the sails cross themselves. An ordered come about or jibe takes 3.5 seconds; the one that does not suit the point of sail means the long way round, as in a boat.
↑ launch the spinnaker, ↓ bring it down
The spinnaker only goes up with the wind abaft the beam: if the bearing relative to the wind is under 90° - on a beat, on a reach, or while she is going about - the launch is refused and the banner says so. Ease her off, then set it. A kite already drawing stays up until it is doused.
space + ← ease the jib
space + → trim the jib in
space + ↑ trim the main in
space + ↓ ease the main
The two bars at the foot of your panel are the sheets, and they are sliders: drag one and its sheet goes exactly where you put it, which is the only trim that is absolute — a key or a touch button only ever winds the sheet in or lets it out at the winch's rate, so it takes time and it takes judgement. The label above each bar still prints the sheet's name and where it is, and the telltales under them still say whether the sail is drawing. Let go and the keyboard is the helm's again; take the sheet back with the keys or the spoken “trim main” / “trim jib” and the bar follows the boat rather than setting it.
C, or the spoken “zoom in”, one step in: your boat and the water around her fill the window
[ / ] step the magnifier in and out - in every phase and from either view, the pre-start included, so the two keys are never dead: from the whole bay a step in is the way into the magnifier (it starts at 3×), and a step out of the smallest factor is the whole bay again
F, or the spoken “zoom out”, the whole bay, full screen, however far in you are
M the voice commands and the microphone on or off (the same switch as the button above), at any time in the race
shift + M the chart one way or the other: the aerial photograph of the real bay, or the drawn chart
V wind arrows on the water
I held down: the information screen - the course, the wind, the rules and this list, for as long as the key is down
Host: in the pre-start, drag the windward mark W, the leeward mark L, the orange starting mark S and the committee end of the line (drag its middle to move the whole line) · shift + R puts the course back · then Enter (or the button in the middle of the bay) fires the sequence
Host: at sea, once every boat has crossed the line, the line is his again: drag its middle or either end and the finish moves with it — the two marks stay where he laid them
Host: the time factor card under the wind panel, 1× to 5×, speeds the boats up — and only the boats: the clock, the wind and the water keep real time
R back to the setup screen: the race settings card, where the wind, the name and host or join are set again - the race in hand stops with it · shift + R is what R was: at sea back to the pre-start, boats re-laid, course kept
Over the line early: a boat across the starting line before the gun is over early, and the whole fleet is recalled — the call is “Over the line, general recall. restart in one minute”, the horn sounds again as the new sequence's warning signal, every boat goes back behind the line and the one minute countdown starts over from there. A boat still over the line when the gun goes is flagged OCS: she comes back behind the line and crosses it again to be racing.
The course: start behind the line and cross it to the course side, beat to the windward mark W and round it leaving it to port, run to the leeward mark L and round that to port too, then finish by crossing the start/finish line — either way through it. A mark rounded the wrong way has not been rounded: the leg stands, the banner says which way the course goes, and the boat comes back and rounds it again. The line is laid across the wind with the orange starting mark S on its west end and the committee boat on its east end. The host lays all of it, and only the host — or the one keyboard that is running both boats: a guest's page follows his, the course, the clock and the flags all arriving in the host's snapshots, so a guest can neither lay the course nor fire the sequence (his Enter says so rather than starting a second countdown of his own).
The signals: a horn at 60 seconds (the warning signal), an air horn beep at 10 seconds and then a beep at 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1, the cannon at the gun — and the smoke goes up off the committee boat's gun with it — and a loud cannon with the bay's cheering for the first boat to finish.
The two boats are crewed from two devices, and both use this one command set: your keys drive your own boat, and your opponent's keys drive theirs. There is nothing to tell the two layouts apart any more. The two hulls are told apart by their sails: the first boat's main and jib are blue and the second boat's are red, and her name plate and her panel in the HUD are in the same colour. A wire that goes under a race does not end it: the race is the host's, so a lost connection costs the second boat nothing but the wire — she holds the last position she was sent, her helm keeps being read, her page dials the room again until it answers, and both boats sail on — and nobody is sent back to the join card by a hiccup, a sleeping phone or a general recall.
Voice (Chrome and Edge; the switch is the button above, on the splash screen, or M at any time in the race — M is in the command box): “come about” · “jibe” · “zoom in” · “zoom out” · “spinnaker” · “spinnaker down” · “trim jib” · “trim main”. Each one presses the key beside it, and the banner shows what was heard - at half the size of the racing banners, so it does not cover the boat; there is no “magnify”: C, or the spoken “zoom in”, magnifies one step in, [ and ] step the magnifier in and out - in every phase and from either view, the pre-start included, so the two keys are never dead: from the whole bay a step in is the way into the magnifier (it starts at 3×), and a step out of the smallest factor is the whole bay again - and F, or the spoken “zoom out”, puts the whole bay back - full screen, however far in you are. The two trims set that sail at the best trim for the point of sail she is on, which is more than a press of the sheet keys can do. The vocabulary is closed: the browser's recogniser is not given a grammar (no browser will take one), so the game holds the list instead - a phrase has to be one of those, or close enough to one of those that the nearest match is unmistakable, and anything else is refused and shown back. Nothing is guessed at with the boat. The microphone is asked for once, when the switch goes on, and never by a timer: while the option is on the page holds the capture open, which is what stops the browser asking again for every phrase, and no recognition session asks for it either. If the browser releases it the page stops listening and says so rather than asking again — M off and on arms one more ask. The come-about command is spoken “come about”, not “tack”. Physics: the Lightning class data, the planing band and the model that boat speed comes out of are on the card behind Click for physics on the race settings card
The boats tack and jibe themselves when the bow or stern crosses the wind - the sails cross to the same trim on the new side - and T/J order the same thing on the spot. Trim matters - watch the telltales: good luffing stalled.
Runs entirely in the browser. Multiplayer uses WebRTC (PeerJS): the host holds the authoritative simulation and guests send their controls. Needs internet for the handshake.
